papers.title: Optical clocks at sea
papers.version: Journal HTML, version of record
papers.region: US; New Zealand ship; TTCP UK relevance
papers.contribution: Integrated iodine-vapour optical clock and microwave frequency-comb output; field timing experiment [S10 Main; Methods].
papers.method: Three clock comparison at NIST against ST05/AT1, then co-located shipboard pairwise comparisons; three-cornered-hat extraction at short times, long-time equal-contribution upper bound [S10 Figs.1–3; Methods Clock comparison].
papers.result: 35 L physics/comb/control package, 26 kg, ~85 W excluding external supply. PICKLES–EPIC pair at sea: 8×10^-15 instability at 100,000 s (~400 ps equivalent daily holdover), without drift correction [S10 Fig.3d; Main].
papers.limitations: Air-conditioned shipping container; no independent high-performance reference at sea; potential correlated environmental noise acknowledged. papers.replication: Different clock ensemble at same RIMPAC campaign supplies architecture-level corroboration, not independent replication of this instrument [S11 Maritime demonstration; S10 Fig.3].
papers.data_code: Raw/processed data on request; analysis routines on reasonable request, not a public archive [S10 Data availability; Code availability].
papers.conflicts: Authors declare no competing interests, but author affiliations include Vector Atomic; commercial participation must remain visible [S10 Author information; Competing interests].
papers.relevance: Analysis: credible local timing holdover evidence; no GNSS-free position solution or deployable network is measured [S10 Figs.1–3].
papers.assessment: Analysis: credible local timing holdover evidence; no GNSS-free position solution or deployable network is measured [S10 Figs.1–3].

papers.title: Atom interferometry at arbitrary orientations and rotation rates
papers.version: Journal HTML, version of record; preprint v1 also inspected
papers.contribution: Combines atomic/classical sensing and actively steered mirror to retain interferometer contrast during rotations [S12 Results; Fig.3].
papers.method: 87Rb Raman Mach–Zehnder, classical mirror accelerometer and two FOGs, manually rotated platform. Acceleration phase is servo-cancelled; rotational phase reconstructed with inertial model [S12 Results; Methods Closed-loop mode].
papers.result: 24 micro-g per-shot inferred sensitivity at 2T=20 ms; tilt 0–30 degrees, rotation up to 14 deg/s. Fringe SNR 5.3 versus 20–30 static [S12 Fig.3; Results Rotation compensation].

Uncharacterized classical sensor response and platform resonances degrade SNR. Full triad/long-term stability remains future work [S12 Methods; Discussion].
papers.replication: Single-instrument study with model/data agreement; no independently reproduced full navigation solution [S12 Figs.2–4; Discussion].

papers.conflicts: Four authors employed by Exail, which commercializes atom-interferometric gravimeters; other authors declare none [S12 Competing interests].

papers.assessment: Analysis: enabling motion-compensation result, not field navigation accuracy or classical-free autonomy [S12 Results; Discussion].

papers.title: Quantum sensing for gravity cartography
papers.version: Nature version of record incl. Methods/Extended Data; first preprint date verified from Research Square manuscript cover p.2, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-882491/v1
papers.contribution: Stray and colleagues demonstrate an outdoor gravity-gradient survey rather than an entanglement-enhanced detector. Two vertically separated rubidium interferometers reject common vibration; a displaced test mass gives 205 ± 13.1 E against a 202 E prediction. Outdoor sensitivity is 466 ± 8 E/√Hz, reaching 20 E statistical uncertainty in ten minutes. [S30 p.591, Figs.1c–2] The survey crosses a known tunnel with a 2 m × 2 m internal section on an 8.5 m line sampled every 0.5 m. Plans, ground-penetrating radar and topography inform the site model. [S30 pp.591–592] Thus this is a substantial field result, but not a blind search for an unknown tunnel. *Analysis*: the distinction matters when translating an anomaly-detection experiment into an intelligence-surveillance claim.
papers.method: The reported SNR of approximately eight divides the estimated 150 E signal by the mean survey error of 17.9 E. Base-station measurements remove drift; ellipse fits failing a specified quality threshold are discarded, leaving 98.4% usable data. [S30 Methods, PDF p.7] Bayesian inversion estimates the horizontal centre at 0.19 ± 0.19 m and surface-to-centre depth at 1.89 m with asymmetric −0.59/+2.3 m uncertainty. [S30 Methods, PDF p.8] The density prior is explicitly informative, whereas the horizontal-centre prior spans the measurement line; the tunnel dimensions are not simply fixed in this inversion. [S30 Extended Data Table 2] *Analysis*: depth and shape remain much less identifiable than horizontal position.
papers.result: See located claims below.
papers.limitations: Survey repeatability is similar to commercial gravimeters and limited by systematics, including Coriolis effects; the proposed fifteen-minute scan is conditional on addressing these effects. [S30 p.593] The approximately 75 kg head plus 250 kg control cases draw approximately 800 W. [S30 Extended Data Fig.2] Data and code are deposited; patents and commercial/government interests are declared. [S30 Methods, PDF p.8] *Analysis*: prioritise independent blind, multi-site surveys with false alarms and complete logistical cost. Scientific confidence is high for this demonstrated anomaly; readiness for unconstrained underground discovery remains conditional.

papers.title: Quantum advantage in microwave quantum radar
papers.version: arXiv:2211.05684v2 (2023-03-02), supplement included; journal metadata checked
papers.type: published journal study; reviewed preprint manuscript
papers.contribution: Assouly and colleagues implement the critical joint measurement missing from earlier microwave correlation demonstrations. An initially entangled probe and stored idler are recombined in a superconducting circuit, and qubit-assisted photon counting estimates whether the target is present. The measured advantage is Q = 1.2 ± 0.1 in an error-exponent metric relative to the calculated optimal coherent-state bound under the same calibrated photon resources. [S31 PDF pp.1–4, Fig.3] This is a stronger scientific benchmark than outperforming one deliberately noisy classical apparatus. *Analysis*: it does not establish superiority to a conventional radar allowed to choose its transmitted power or operating scenario.
papers.method: The hardware operates at 15 mK. Its target is a controllable notch filter and 12 m coaxial delay, rather than an outdoor object; position, speed and reflectivity are assumed known. [S31 PDF pp.1–2, Fig.1] Signal/noise photon populations and target reflectivity are measured with dedicated calibration protocols. The highlighted data use fifteen series of 500,000 attempts, with signal and noise recalibrated between series. [S31 PDF pp.3–4, Fig.3] Thermal noise is switched on after state preparation. [S31 PDF p.2] *Analysis*: these controls make the proof interpretable but deliberately avoid several environmental and target-search difficulties.
papers.result: See located claims below.
papers.limitations: The supplement explicitly says photon-population fitting uncertainties are mostly statistical and omit measurement-protocol imperfections; reflectivity uncertainty is checked across probe amplitudes. [S31 supplement F, PDF p.11] The model underestimates measured advantage, with the origin unresolved; initial thermal populations shrink the region supporting advantage. [S31 PDF pp.4–5, Fig.4] *Analysis*: these are calibration/model qualifications, not evidence that the result is false. A high-confidence application assessment would require independent calibration validation and real targets with unknown delays.
papers.replication: No independent experimental replication established in this bounded scan; no experiments rerun.
papers.data_code: Journal figure source-data links checked; no code execution.
papers.conflicts: EU QMICS funding and IARPA/Lincoln Labs supplied hardware, PDF p.5 acknowledgments; no competing-interest declaration located in examined preprint.
papers.relevance: Analysis: RF awareness and/or radar evidence discipline
papers.assessment: The journal page provides figure source data; this review did not execute an independent analysis or find an independent experimental replication. [S31 journal page, Source data] *Analysis*: prioritise as a credible entanglement-assisted detection experiment and an engineering-warning case, not as demonstrated long-range or stealth-target radar.

papers.title: Waveguide-coupled Rydberg spectrum analyzer from 0 to 20 GHz
papers.type: published journal study; reviewed preprint manuscript
papers.contribution: Meyer, Kunz and Cox demonstrate a Rydberg receiver backend coupled to a microwave waveguide, with an external antenna used to collect ambient signals. This is atomic transduction and heterodyne reception, not an entanglement-generated radar advantage. The system covers carrier tuning from DC to 20 GHz, while the instantaneous 3 dB bandwidth is 4 MHz. Its abstract reports intrinsic sensitivity up to −120 ± 2 dBm/Hz and over 80 dB linear dynamic range. [S32 PDF pp.1,4, Fig.3] *Analysis*: the broad carrier range must not be described as simultaneous twenty-gigahertz reception bandwidth.
papers.method: Figure 1 distinguishes directly measured sensitivity, a photon-shot-noise-limited value obtained after independent subtraction of laser phase noise, and preamplified sensitivity. The preamplifier sensitivity curves are calculated by referring intrinsic noise to the input and combining amplifier noise, although ambient reception itself is demonstrated with amplification. [S32 PDF pp.2–3, Fig.1; p.5, Fig.4] The strongest headline figures therefore need the measurement category attached. *Analysis*: a backend improvement cannot be credited with the entire antenna/amplifier chain's performance.
papers.result: See located claims below.
papers.limitations: A conventional rabbit-ears antenna feeds the system; AM/FM and Wi-Fi/Bluetooth examples appear in the laboratory, including audio verification of one AM station. [S32 PDF pp.4–5] The atom chamber is approximately 50 °C, the coupling beam is approximately 500 mW, and optical path and power fluctuations are actively stabilised. [S32 Appendix A, PDF p.7] These details qualify the phrase near-room-temperature: cryogenics are avoided, but lasers and control are still necessary.
papers.replication: No independent experimental replication established in this bounded scan; no experiments rerun.
papers.data_code: No explicit public data/code statement located in examined manuscript.
papers.conflicts: Army authors; partial DARPA support, PDF p.6 acknowledgments.
papers.relevance: Analysis: RF awareness and/or radar evidence discipline
papers.assessment: The waveguide's measured transmission deteriorated over seven months, attributed provisionally to rubidium contamination; reported sensitivities retain waveguide losses rather than subtracting them. [S32 Appendix D, PDF p.8] This is a disclosed durability issue, not a confirmed failure mechanism. *Analysis*: useful next tests are stability, calibration and power accounting against an equally broadband classical backend under matched antenna conditions. No data/code availability statement was located in the examined manuscript; no independent replication was established in this bounded scan. *Analysis*: confidence is medium in integrated reception, lower in claims of surpassing established receiver limits. Detailed source confidence retains the reviewed-manuscript version caveat.

papers.title: Performance of antenna-based and Rydberg quantum RF sensors in the electrically small regime
papers.version: Applied Physics Letters version of record
papers.contribution: Backes and colleagues provide a consequential baseline correction: comparison with a passive unmatched antenna can overstate the attraction of an atomic receiver. Their equivalent-circuit analysis compares similarly sized dipole/loop antennas with matched passive, unmatched passive and active readout against warm-vapour EIT and ideal standard-quantum-limit Rydberg sensing. The example uses approximately 1 cm sensors over 30 kHz–30 MHz. [S33 article pp.144002-1–3, Figs.1–3] *Analysis*: this is a theoretical comparison with literature experimental points, not a new matched field trial demonstrating defeat of every Rydberg architecture.
papers.method: The active classical example uses a high-impedance amplifier with 1 nV/√Hz input voltage noise and 100 MΩ input impedance. All sensors are assigned dipolar directivity, so incoming atmospheric noise affects their external signal-to-noise ratio equivalently. [S33 pp.144002-2–3, Eqs.1,7] Under these assumptions, active unmatched dipoles exceed contemporary warm-vapour EIT sensitivity. [S33 p.144002-4, Fig.3] *Analysis*: electrically small size alone is insufficient justification for comparison only against inefficient passive antennas; classical active electronics must receive equal engineering attention.
papers.result: See located claims below.
papers.limitations: The most spectacular atomic bound instead assumes tightly packed cold atoms, optimised transitions, a restricted interaction-induced shift, and large atom numbers. The authors warn that collective effects could limit this idealisation and that it is likely physically unrealizable, paralleling the ideal matched dipole bound. [S33 p.144002-4] Typical atmospheric noise also sits above the ideal limits. [S33 Fig.3 and p.144002-4] *Analysis*: a quieter internal detector cannot remove the same external field noise it measures; sheltered metrology and arrays require different operational cases.
papers.replication: No independent experimental replication established in this bounded scan; no experiments rerun.
papers.data_code: Notebook/Python/data described in supplementary material, article p.144002-5; supplement not retrieved.
papers.conflicts: No conflicts declared; DHS/MITRE/Army support disclosed, article p.144002-5.
papers.relevance: Analysis: RF awareness and/or radar evidence discipline
papers.assessment: The supplement is described as containing the figure-generating notebook, Python and data; declared conflicts are absent, while DHS/MITRE/Army affiliations and funding are disclosed. [S33 p.144002-5] The supplement itself was not retrieved here. *Analysis*: confidence is high in the paper's stated comparison within its model, moderate in transfer to complete deployed systems. Its value is methodological discipline: require frequency, size, bandwidth, amplification and ambient-noise assumptions before accepting receiver advantage.

papers.title: Electrometry of extremely-low frequencies from kHz to sub-Hz with a Rydberg-atom sensor
papers.version: EPJ Quantum Technology 13:87 version of record
papers.contribution: Chandra, Paensin and Dumke extend low-frequency Rydberg electrometry with a paraffin-coated caesium cell, auxiliary field reversal and lock-in detection. The laboratory observes applied electric fields between 0.5 Hz and 10 kHz. The reported sensitivity is 819 μV/cm/√Hz at 1 Hz, 33 at 10 Hz, 10 at 100 Hz and 2 at 1 kHz. [S34 pp.1,8–9, Figs.4–5] This is an atomic electric-field receiver improvement, not entanglement-enhanced target detection. *Analysis*: it is relevant to difficult low-frequency sensing but cannot by itself establish underground or underwater detection range.
papers.method: Coated and uncoated-cell transient controls show slower screening in the coated cell. The proposed microscopic explanation is expressly qualitative and charge transport is not directly measured. [S34 pp.4–6, Fig.2] Residual screening remains and reduces low-frequency responsivity. [S34 p.8] Fields are generated by external copper plates; the term electrode-free means no electrodes inserted into the vapour, rather than no electrodes in the experiment. [S34 pp.3–4, Fig.1] *Analysis*: retaining this distinction prevents a misleading impression of a passive stand-alone receiver.
papers.result: See located claims below.
papers.limitations: Sensitivity is estimated from responsivity and combined photodetector/lock-in noise. The classical curve is theoretically estimated for a 3 cm dipole, referenced to an earlier assessment, rather than experimentally measured alongside the atoms. [S34 p.9, Fig.5] The sensor uses room-temperature vapour but a high-finesse cavity locks two lasers; a strong auxiliary field sets the operating point. [S34 pp.3,7,10–13] *Analysis*: the claimed size-based advantage should be tested against an active classical receiver and complete-system size/power, especially given the separate baseline analysis in S33.
papers.replication: No independent experimental replication established in this bounded scan; no experiments rerun.
papers.data_code: Data on reasonable request, p.16; no code archive located.
papers.conflicts: No competing interests; Singapore NRF/A*STAR support, p.16.
papers.relevance: Analysis: RF awareness and/or radar evidence discipline
papers.assessment: The authors identify laser intensity drift as a present limit and explicitly require further outdoor pickup, ground-loop and thermal/polarisation control before field deployment. [S34 pp.9–10] Data are available on reasonable request; no competing interests are declared. [S34 p.16] *Analysis*: confidence is high for controlled low-frequency response, moderate for its sensitivity estimate and low for operational advantage pending matched practical comparison. No independent replication was established in this bounded scan.

papers.title: A Note on the Efficient Operation of Quantum Radar and the Fair Classical Comparison
papers.version: IEEE Transactions on Radar Systems version of record, pp.875–880
papers.contribution: Bischeltsrieder and colleagues analyse a specific two-mode-squeezed-vacuum correlation receiver and separate outperforming a classical comparator from efficiently reaching a chosen detection error. papers.review:
Goto and colleagues introduce ballistic and discrete simulated bifurcation, numerical classical dynamics inspired by nonlinear quantum oscillators. Inelastic walls improve convergence; sign discretisation suppresses continuous-variable errors. The paper compares FPGA implementations and larger GPU calculations with other Ising machines. Its K2000 result is target time-to-target of 0.26 ms for bSB and optimal/best-known time-to-solution of 1.3 s for dSB, using a 99% success criterion. These metrics answer different questions. [S50 Results, Fig.3]

The large-scale demonstration is valuable, but the million-spin claim needs care: the GPU experiments use statistically estimated reference energies rather than certified instance optima. The 16-GPU implementation combines an algorithmic improvement with substantial parallel hardware. Other-machine results were cited or estimated from literature because the authors lacked access; some comparators were older hardware or simulator predictions. The time step was selected from five values and step counts optimised separately for the target metric. [S50 Results, Fig.4; Benchmarking; Methods]

*Analysis:* this establishes a useful competitive classical baseline, not a general theorem that quantum-inspired dynamics win. The central method is explicit enough to reconstruct, but independent matched-budget replication, tuned contemporary classical heuristics, and native constrained scheduling comparisons would strengthen transfer. End-to-end formulation and constraint feasibility are absent from these Ising tests. Toshiba employment and a declared patent interest warrant recording without dismissing the equations or results. [S50 Competing interests; Discussion]

The full main article was reviewed; the separately hosted supplement was not retrieved. Consequently its detailed FPGA resource and comparator reconstruction tables remain an access gap. *Analysis:* retain this as a historical methods anchor, with deployment confidence low.

papers.review:
This benchmark is most useful for its changing winners: HSS leads the mixed MQLib set, DA leads the tested NAE-3SAT regime, and SBM leads SK spin glasses. The five-minute MQLib experiment counts ties, producing 22 HSS, 20 DA, 16 SBM and seven SA wins; these are comparative wins rather than optimum certificates. Its score uses the best observed energy among the four solvers. [S51 pp.3–7, Eq.4, Figs.1–3]

The comparator is D-Wave neal SA on one i9-9900K CPU thread, against specialised or cloud systems. SBM automatically searches parameters; its evaluation build is proprietary. HSS internals are closed, so the benchmark cannot isolate any QPU contribution. Time is also heterogeneous: requested HSS/SBM budgets, reported DA elapsed time, and locally measured SA sampling time; network communication is excluded. [S51 pp.2–3]

*Analysis:* the paper supports problem-dependent solver selection, but provides a weak basis for a blanket claim that these services beat competitive classical optimisation. Equal wall-clock allocations on unspecified unequal compute resources are not equal resource budgets. An operational follow-up should add tuned parallel tempering, modern QUBO/local-search portfolios and native mathematical models, reporting feasibility and true business objectives rather than only encoded energy.

The MQLib set comprises 45 instances inherited from HSS’s white-paper selection; synthetic tests average ten NAE-3SAT and six SK instances, with independent runs for plotted points. Public instance generators help reproducibility, but additional data are request-only and service internals remain opaque. D-Wave and Toshiba research support is acknowledged despite a no-conflicts declaration. [S51 pp.2,7,9–10] *Analysis:* confidence is moderate for the reported ranking on these configurations and low for broad logistical superiority.

papers.review:
The case study models robot movements and laboratory processing motivated by BASF, comparing a QUBO with two native Gurobi MIPs. This is a stronger application comparison than forcing every solver through the same QUBO. Its 260 generated instances split into 161 minor cases with 2,071–8,080 QUBO variables and 99 major cases with 10,822–22,692. [S52 §§2–3, Table1]

The crucial contribution is equal-quality timing: Gurobi’s progress log identifies when it first matches each heuristic’s final objective, avoiding comparison of heuristic approximation time with exact optimality-proof time. Sequence Gurobi reaches DA quality 10–100 times faster on minor instances; the hybrid DA is faster at comparable quality for the largest 20-sample instances. Gurobi still generally finds better final objectives. Some D-Wave hybrid outputs are infeasible. [S52 §4.1, Figs.3–5; §4.2, Figs.6–7]

Reported end-to-end time includes network delays from submission to solution return but excludes constructing the optimisation model. Major-instance Gurobi equal-quality times are capped at 3,600 seconds when the target is not reached; this is censoring rather than a measured matching time. DA hybrid budgets were allocated from five hours, approximately proportional to variable count. The comparator is an out-of-box solver; tailored metaheuristics were explicitly excluded. [S52 §§3.2,4.1]

*Analysis:* this supports a bounded positive case for specialised classical annealing in large constrained scheduling, while preserving a strong negative result for smaller problems. Near-constant heuristic runtimes are partly budget choices, so they do not establish superior asymptotic complexity. Transfer to defence logistics requires representative constraints, repeated-run uncertainty, tuned classical alternatives, and model-construction costs. The paper itself describes a technology snapshot rather than general advantage. [S52 §5]

papers.review:
This is the revised, published successor to the 2025 preprint titled “Closing the Quantum-Classical Scaling Gap”; using its old title or calling it unreviewed would misstate the source. The reviewed v2 is dated 10 July 2026 and links to Physical Review Applied 26, 014024. [S53 arXiv identity/version; journal DOI]

The authors test the same Sidon-28 QAC-graph instances as the challenged study: 125 per size, 142–1,322 variables, and 100 independent solver runs. They optimise simulated-bifurcation steps and parallel replicas against a 99%-success time-to-epsilon metric, with original reference ground energies certified using Gurobi. GPU SBM closes the reported scaling gap on these problems. Larger classical instances extend to 38,320 variables, beyond the tested QPU range. [S53 main text, Eq.1, Figs.1–3]

The supplement distinguishes GPU compute time, total CPU/GPU execution, QPU access and externally measured runtime. Common initialization costs are nevertheless omitted; GPU replicas execute together whereas annealer samples are sequential. Sparse 3D spin glasses retain favourable quantum annealing-time scaling, but current operational overhead prevents demonstrated practical scaling advantage. [S53 S5–S7; Fig.4]

*Analysis:* the strongest conclusion is that the earlier classical baseline was insufficient and runtime accounting can change the verdict. It is not evidence that SBM dominates every sparse instance, nor that fits at relaxed energy targets establish exact-optimisation complexity. Tuning steps and replicas is legitimate but its search budget should accompany operational procurement comparisons. Extended-size classical success does not directly measure a future QPU. Quantumz.io affiliations and request-only new data constrain independence and reproducibility. [S53 acknowledgments/data availability] *Analysis:* high confidence in the need for this baseline, moderate in generalisation beyond this benchmark.

claims.text: Largest5376-spin Pegasus TN runs require local dimension reduction to2^16 states due to memory.
Reference dE=(E-Ebest)/(2|Ebest|) uses combined solver best when true ground unknown.
Planted cases improve best-energy difference by factor3–4; ground states not found for721/3065-spin cases.

papers.review:
This study makes tensor-network failure an object of investigation rather than hiding it behind selected successes. The method combines approximate marginals with branch-and-bound, sparse PEPS representations and GPU computation. Twenty instances per selected size underpin the comparisons; random Pegasus and Zephyr graphs test more difficult connectivity than earlier Chimera examples. [S54 §§III–V, Fig.10]

At 5,376 Pegasus spins, memory forces local state reduction to 2^16 configurations per cluster. On the tested random problems, TN is slower and returns worse energies than SBM/QA; planted square-lattice cases embedded into Pegasus reverse the quality ranking, improving the best-energy gap by a factor of three to four. The larger planted cases still do not reach their known ground states. Thus the negative finding is geometry and instance dependent. [S54 §V.3; AppendixA, Fig.A1]

The error measure is dE=(E−Ebest)/(2|Ebest|), and Ebest pools solver outputs when ground truth is unknown. This must not be silently relabelled as a conventional certified optimality gap. A 216-spin diagnostic shows a trade-off between low-temperature search resolution and approximate contraction stability; dimensional preprocessing can itself remove the optimum. [S54 §V.2, Eq.14; §VI, Fig.12]

*Analysis:* this is persuasive evidence of a concrete limitation in this implementation, not a no-go theorem for tensor networks. Sampling diversity is separately assessed and cannot be inferred from one best-energy result. Runtime comparisons also need cloud-access overhead and hardware budgets before operational interpretation. Open Julia code and an instance/results repository make this relatively reproducible, though neither was executed here. [S54 §VII; Data availability; AppendicesD–E] *Analysis:* useful for screening solver proposals, with no demonstrated constrained-logistics deployment.

papers.review:
Safi and colleagues compare industrially motivated scheduling across IBM, D-Wave, Fujitsu DA and classical approaches. Their QUBOs encode job-to-machine assignments; sequencing remains classical. Constraint-rich and compact formulations deliberately trade fidelity against solvability. DA reaches more than 10,000 logical variables, while current quantum devices are limited to small cases, and QUBO compilation choices materially affect DA validity. [S55 §§III,V–VI]

The reference-quality caveat is decisive: the exact branch-and-bound solver certifies small cases only, with the largest tractable example at six machines, five rigs and 14 jobs. Larger references are the best found within one hour, although some figures use optimal-reference language. DA exceeds the tested greedy/iterative approximations; this does not establish superiority over a broadly tuned classical portfolio. [S55 §V-A; §VI-D, Fig.8; §VII-C]

Runtime also needs correction before reuse. Section V-C labels a metric end-to-end execution time, but Section VII-E explicitly excludes communication latency, API overhead and queues. The authors further acknowledge realistic data are not drawn directly from live production and omit dynamic arrivals. Outputs from DA and hybrid D-Wave expose limited top solutions rather than full sample distributions. [S55 §§V-C,VII-B,VII-E]

*Analysis:* the useful result concerns formulation, feasibility and specialised classical hardware, not an operational quantum speedup. Claiming DA as a lower bound for future fault-tolerant annealing is an assumption, not an experimental result; the authors themselves note DA’s separate constraint handling is unavailable on current physical annealers. [S55 §VII-B] The v1 preprint and claimed reproduction package warrant independent review before high-confidence adoption. *Analysis:* moderate confidence in configuration-specific engineering lessons, low in universal solver ranking or live scheduling advantage.

papers.contribution: Nonlinear Zeeman dynamics create intrinsic single-atom squeezing; optimized dynamical decoupling locks its changing axis to the observable instead of simply suppressing that dynamics.
papers.method: Breit–Rabi expansion yields a quadratic spin Hamiltonian. A differential-evolution algorithm chooses discretized RF rotation pulses. Numerical state fidelity and signal/noise propagation assess dark-interval and continuous-readout protocols; supplementary notes derive SQL and the nuclear-electron entanglement mechanism.
papers.result: Modelled87Rb maximum metrological gain approaches2.9dB. Under assumed1cm³ room-temperature cell,N=1.42e10 and10ms coherence, Discussion calculates4.29fT/sqrt(Hz) versus5.99fT/sqrt(Hz) CSS SQL and14.04fT/sqrt(Hz) NLZ-degraded reference. These are predictions, not recorded instrument sensitivity.
papers.limitations: Explicitly no atom–atom entanglement is needed; gain is single-atom nuclear-electron correlation and independent ofN. The largest apparent improvement also restores assumed coherence, not squeezing alone. Instantaneous-rotation and rotating-wave approximations constrain pulse duration. Readout backaction, gradients and measurement-duty trade-offs are discussed but no complete measured noise budget or moving-platform demonstration is supplied.
papers.replication: Main Results,Methods,Discussion and supplementary notes1–3,8 inspected. Equations and optimized pulse sequence are given; authors say evaluation data are within paper/supplement and additional data on request. No code repository identified; no experimental replication established because this is a proposed protocol.

papers.title: Superabsorption in an organic microcavity: Toward a quantum battery
papers.version: arxiv full manuscript; journal metadata cross-checked
papers.type: published journal study; reviewed preprint manuscript
papers.contribution: Organic-molecule collective light–matter coupling produces faster absorption as absorber count increases; dephasing moves energy into less radiative dark modes.
papers.method: Lumogen-F Orange dye in polystyrene is placed between dielectric mirrors. Concentrations0.5%,1%,5%,10% span weak to strong coupling. Femtosecond pump–probe differential reflectivity is fit to an open-system model; peak population-derived energy density, rise time and charging power are extracted from model fits, with supporting spectroscopy and fit sensitivity in supplement.
papers.result: Spectroscopy supports superextensive charging and storage-capacity behaviour over tested regimes; scaling varies with coupling/decay regime. Only6–8% of initial pump energy enters the cavity according to reflectivity estimates. The observed energy is molecular excitation, not delivered electrical energy.
papers.limitations: This precursor has no demonstrated electrical extraction, useful discharge cycle or net wall-plug efficiency. Increased concentration and coupling regimes change together; fitted collective dynamics should not be reported as proof that entanglement uniquely causes practical energy advantage. Finite experimental concentration range, molecular quenching at larger concentration and dephasing/decay assumptions limit extrapolation. A fixed-resource comparison requires incident/absorbed energy,mode volume,loss and preparation accounting.
papers.replication: Full accessible arxiv PDF main text plus supplement examined; DOI/journal identity verified through opened publisher DOI and author university research portal. Version is latest downloadable arxiv manuscript, not an independently diffed journal PDF. Detailed fabrication,spectroscopy and fitting documented; independent replication/open code repository not established in this bounded review.

papers.title: Superextensive electrical power from a quantum battery
papers.version: Journal HTML
papers.access: full text and methods; supplement where provided
papers.contribution: Charge-transport layers turn an organic polariton microcavity into a steady-state electrical-output device, addressing the missing extraction step in earlier spectroscopy-only battery demonstrations.
papers.method: Eight CuPc:C60 devices vary absorber count within a nominal126nm cavity. Cavity and no-cavity controls share substrates. Reflectance establishes strong coupling; ultrafast pump–probe data quantify excitation dynamics; current–voltage scans under625nm illumination measure electrical output. Intersystem crossing populates metastable triplet states; coupled-oscillator and open-system models connect these stages.
papers.result: Maximum electrical power density is roughly10–40microW/cm². The ratio of cavity/no-cavity peak power increases withN; authors interpret this as superextensive output, with modelPc~N². Optical excited-state signals persist tens of nanoseconds; the six-orders-of-magnitude ratio compares to charging times, not hours or years of storage.
papers.limitations: Always-illuminated steady-state photocurrent does not by itself demonstrate sustained useful dark discharge. Controls omit a metal mirror and therefore differ optically as well as in coupling; comparisons to an independently optimized photovoltaic architecture and equal absorbed/incident energy are needed for practical superiority. Concentration alters carrier dynamics,cavity detuning andQ; authors normalize with same-run controls and discussD8 deviation. No entanglement witness isolates uniquely quantum causal advantage. No complete round-trip/net external efficiency,macroscopic capacity or cycling durability demonstrated.
papers.replication: Full journal text,Methods and32-page supplement inspected, emphasizing geometry/controls,ultrafast normalization and electrical model. Data available on request; no public code repository identified. Independent replication not established.
papers.data_code: Full journal text,Methods and32-page supplement inspected, emphasizing geometry/controls,ultrafast normalization and electrical model. Data available on request; no public code repository identified. Independent replication not established.
papers.conflicts: Authors declare no competing interests.
papers.relevance: Analysis: worthwhile frontier test in low-light harvesting rather than evidence for near-term defence energy storage. Require dark-discharge energy,integrated photon-to-electric efficiency and optimized equal-resource classical controls.
papers.assessment: High confidence in measured electrical output; medium confidence in causal scaling interpretation; low deployment maturity.
